items.summary_raw:
The handover marks the end of a 13-year licence for Smart DCC, a subsidiary of Capita, after years of spiralling costs and delays

Control over Great Britain’s 39m smart meters has passed to a non-profit startup after its former owner presided over more than a decade of spiralling costs and delays in the troubled network.

The company owned by crisis-hit outsourcing firm Capita has promised a “seamless transition” to its not-for-profit successor, which will take over running the data network connecting the smart meters from this week.

items.title: ‘They have schedules to follow’: how fast ferries can threaten endangered whales in the Mediterranean
items.summary_raw:
A Guardian investigation has found that despite a recommendation to slow down, leading shipping companies continue to travel above advised speeds in a key habitat for cetaceans

Marine biologist Alice Barbarioli waits with her camera trained on the horizon. A few minutes earlier, the hydrophone beneath the Pelagos research vessel detected codas – the sequence of clicks sperm whales use to communicate.

The sperm whale reveals its head and dorsal fin as those onboard the vessel in the Pelagos sanctuary, a conservation area established to protect marine mammals in the north-western Mediterranean, rush to take photos and note the rhythm of its breathing. After a few minutes, the animal arches its back, and begins to head back into the depths of the sea. They wait to catch a glimpse of its tail.

items.title: Cryosphere faces permanent damage when world overshoots 1.5C, scientists warn
items.summary_raw:
UN-backed report finds even temporary rises above Paris agreement target could cause harm to glaciers and polar ice sheets

Earth’s icy regions face such dangerous melting that global heating should be brought back below 1C after an inevitable period of overshooting global temperature targets, a UN report has found.

Permanent and widespread losses of snow and ice expose a “persistent myth” that overshooting the 1.5C target of the Paris climate agreement – to 2C or 3C – could be manageable or even preferable to urgent cuts to emissions, the report found.

Saudi Arabia has condemned the attack on Qatar’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier Al Mayeda and backed measures to protect Qatari vessels and international trade.

In a statement posted on X, the Saudi foreign ministry reiterated its “rejection of all violations that threaten the security and safety of maritime navigation and global energy supplies”.

It urged the international community to act immediately to uphold international law and “ensure maritime security and the safety of international trade”.

The Al Mayeda, owned and operated by the Qatar Gas Transport Company, was struck in the Gulf earlier today.

items.title: Incendiary Attack Targets Thanos Plevris’ Political Office in Central Athens
items.summary_raw:
ATHENS. An incendiary attack targeted the political office of Migration and Asylum Minister Thanos Plevris in the Kolonaki district of central Athens early Sunday, after an improvised explosive device was placed at the entrance to the building. The incident occurred at approximately 2:15 a.m. on Alexandrou Soutsou Street. According to reports, the device consisted of two gas canisters and caused damage to the building’s main entrance, while windows were also shattered. No injuries were reported. Police officers rushed to the scene, along with a team from the Explosive Ordnance Disposal Unit, which examined the site and collected evidence. The investigation has been assigned to the State Security Subdivision of the Attica General Police Directorate. Authorities are examining security camera footage and seeking witnesses to identify those responsible.

items.title: US and Israel Differ on Iran Strike
items.summary_raw:
REPORT: U.S. and Israel Divided Over Scope of Iran Strike
Israeli analyst Peretz says the U.S. and Israel differ over the scope of a potential military operation against Iran.

Israel reportedly favors a broad campaign targeting Iran’s nuclear facilities, ballistic missile capabilities and other strategic assets.

The U.S., however, is said to prefer limited, precision strikes, creating differences over the scale and objectives of a possible operation.

items.title: Mitsotakis: Illegal Turkish-Libyan Memorandum Cannot Erase Greek Islands’ Rights
items.summary_raw:
ATHENS - Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis reiterated on Sunday that the "illegal Turkey-Libya memorandum" cannot override the rights of Greek islands, stressing that a strong Greece must defend its national interests through international law, deterrence and diplomacy. In his weekly review of government work, Mitsotakis referred to his recent visit to New York, where he chaired a UN Security Council meeting on maritime security, highlighting the connection between international diplomacy and the security of Greek citizens. "Peace and respect for international law are prerequisites for progress and for being able to plan our lives with confidence and a sense of security," he said, adding that Greece must act with determination while keeping the door open to dialogue.

The post Mitsotakis: Illegal Turkish-Libyan Memorandum Cannot Erase Greek Islands’ Rights appeared first on The National Herald.

items.title: ‘Bunch of baloney’: calls grow for Cop summit reforms as countries on track to fail nature targets
items.summary_raw:
Cop17, focused on protecting nature and restoring ecosystems, concludes on Saturday with critics saying system allows ‘one idiot’ to stall progress

Calls are growing for major reforms to UN biodiversity summits as countries fail to deliver on their promises to halt the destruction of the natural world, with governments likely on track to continue their record of never having met a target in the 34-year history of the convention.

Two weeks of negotiations at biodiversity Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, concluded on Saturday morning with countries vowing to redouble their efforts to meet this decade’s targets, which include commitments to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore nearly a third of Earth’s degraded ecosystems and reform $500bn (£410bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies.

items.title: Karamanlis: We Will Not Ask Turkey’s Permission for Projects in the Aegean
items.summary_raw:
ATHENS – Kostas Karamanlis, the former prime minister of Greece, in his speech at the War Museum in Athens marking the October 28 anniversary, with former Prime Minister Antonis Samaras also present, emphatically raised issues of national interests, rejecting the logic of mutual concessions in Greek-Turkish relations. He pointed out that any acceptance of Turkish authorization for the electricity interconnection would create a precedent with broader consequences for the Aegean. He was sending a clear message that Greece cannot ask Turkey’s permission for the Kasos-Cyprus cable, a warning about a Turkish plan to control the Aegean up to the 25th parallel, and offered sharp criticism of Western allies over their stance toward Ankara and Cyprus. Kostas Karamanlis placed particular emphasis on the Greece-Cyprus electricity interconnection, linking Turkish interventions to Ankara’s effort to gain a say even in the implementation of a European project.

items.title: The Iran war is deepening the US energy crisis. A bad winter is ahead | Mark Wolfe
items.summary_raw:
Congress must act to ensure that families are able to heat their homes before the start of the season

Heating oil may be the clearest warning yet of how the war in Iran is deepening the US’s energy affordability crisis. Families who heat their homes with oil are facing bills that could be 50% higher this winter, adding nearly $900 to the cost of keeping their homes warm. These families were already struggling before the war began.

As the Guardian recently reported, research by my organization found that electricity shutoffs in 10 states had increased 28% over the past two years. Millions of Americans were already falling behind on their utility bills, forced to choose between paying for energy, food, medicine and rent. Now they face another round of increases in gasoline, electricity and home heating costs.

If the polls can be believed, the US could see a blue wave in the midterms, giving Democrats a chance to take back the House and Senate, and gaining up to four governor’s seats.

These wins could give Democrats new power to resist Donald Trump’s anti-climate agenda, and to push forward climate policies at the state level. But if Republicans maintain power, it could further embolden Trump’s “drill, baby, drill” agenda and leave intact his administration’s latitude to continue dismantling regulatory measures his critics say protect public health and the planet.

items.title: Severe rainfall and flood warnings issued for central Greece and western Turkey
items.summary_raw:
Turkey has been hit by powerful thunderstorms and a fatal tornado this week with more heavy rain expected

Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.

Travelling eastwards towards south Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. items.title: Record-breaking high tides spark chaos – and kayak commutes – across California
items.summary_raw:
Seawater surges into low-lying communities from San Diego to San Francisco Bay Area, submerging streets, homes and businesses

Historic high tides have caused chaos up and down the California coast this week, as parts of the state were inundated by record-breaking water levels. Seawater surged into low-lying communities from San Diego to the San Francisco Bay Area, submerging streets, flooding homes and businesses, and jamming important transportation corridors and train routes.

Kayakers and paddle boarders could be seen gliding through typically busy thoroughfares in Marin county, north of San Francisco, on Monday and Tuesday. Several drivers had to be rescued from floating cars in the area, while cyclists who had attempted to cross the temporary lagoon that had formed quickly found themselves waist-deep. Further south, in cities such as Newport Beach, water pounded the emergency infrastructure set up to keep out the swelling sea, which seeped through berms, seawalls and sandbag blockades along the shoreline.

items.title: Mark Carney is celebrated abroad – while consolidating power at home | Shiri Pasternak
items.summary_raw:
The Canadian prime minister’s reckoning with Trumpism in Davos clashes with his attacks on environmental, Indigenous and labour rights

The Canadian prime minister is a hero around the world for his Davos speech that reckoned with a reconfiguration of power in the shadow of Donald Trump.

But at home, Mark Carney is mirroring the US president by radically centralizing power within his office and cabinet and taking a hatchet to dozens of laws protecting environmental, Indigenous and labour rights, all in order to enact his economic agenda.

Shiri Pasternak is an associate professor in criminology at Toronto Metropolitan University and a member of the Infrastructure Beyond Extractivism research team, a collaboration between critical scholars and Indigenous land defenders across North America

items.summary_raw: LATEST: With 51.8% of votes counted in Israel's election, neither bloc has a majority.  Netanyahu's bloc has 55 seats, the opposition 49 and the Arab-led parties 16, against the 61 needed to govern.  Likud leads the partial count with 27 seats, ahead of Eisenkot's Yashar (21), the Joint List (12), Bennett's Together (11), and The Democrats and United Torah Judaism (9 each).  The overnight exit-poll updates also moved toward Netanyahu.  Kan 11 now gives his bloc 51 seats, Channel 12 gives it 52 and Channel 13 gives it 51, all up from 50, while the opposition dropped to 49–51.  Channel 14, which is close to Netanyahu, is the only one that now projects him a majority, with 62 seats.  The opposition and both Arab parties together would reach 65.  However, the Joint List has offered only outside support, so any anti-Netanyahu government would have to be a minority government or depend on parties from the other bloc.  Netanyahu, for his part, is 6 seats short in the current count, so the remaining 48% of votes and which small parties clear the 3.25% threshold could decide the outcome.

Donald Trump announced his administration is “terminating” Biden-era regulations holding oil and gas companies accountable for large leaks of planet-warming methane during a rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday evening.

Trump said during a campaign rally in Texas that the change would save consumers and energy producers $45bn and unlock 210 million barrels of oil – equivalent to about 10 days of US petroleum consumption. “Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers,” Trump said, lifting what he called “crippling regulations on methane that caused prices to skyrocket” for small oil and gas operators.

items.title: Plan for multibillion-pound Sizewell nuclear plant a ‘terrible deal’ for UK taxpayers, MPs say
items.summary_raw:
The public accounts committee has said the risk to billpayers is ‘extraordinary’

The government’s plan to fund a multibillion-pound nuclear plant at the Sizewell site in Suffolk represents a “terrible deal” for the UK taxpayer over the rest of the century, according to the government’s spending watchdog.

MPs on the public accounts committee (PAC) have warned the government that the cost of the Sizewell C nuclear reactor could spiral to almost £48bn, leaving bill payers on the hook to provide an extra £9.8bn to construct the plant before 2040 and a further £12bn over its 60-year operating life.
